Begin by examining the foliage; a uniform pale yellow on the older leaves signals nitrogen hunger, not a disease. Do not purchase a broad-spectrum NPK fertilizer or a systemic fungicide from the seller because mineral fertilizer alone often fails on run-down soils. Restore organic matter by adding manure, compost, or by leaving residues in the ground rather than burning them. Include a legume like cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level to keep the nitrogen-fixing nodules in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil test and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot.

history.content: What is a basin, in the technical sense used here?

And the catalogue puts basins in the same build as other earthworks: main bund 80 to 100 cm at the lower base, 35 to 40 cm at the top, 30 to 35 cm high, secondary bund 70 to 80, 25 to 30 and 25 to 30. It also gives a fourth use for a bund's spillway: it can carry the excess water from the main bund when it carries too much.

In the catalogue's own definition, it is a low area of the plot that retains water so that the soil can hold it for a limited period, and it gives the two conditions for it: the soil must be able to hold a good amount of water and let it drain well, and it must be able to hold water for a short time. So the basin is the low-lying area that holds its water for a short time. That is what the catalogue offers as an option among the many ways of managing the soil.

history.content: I have a small plot that has been left fallow for a few years and I want to plant yam this rainy season. What steps should I follow?

draws.answer: First, take deep, rested soil that has no striga, or plant a striga tolerant maize variety together with your yam. Then plant the yam in March when the rains are strong. Perform the first weeding about two weeks after sowing. After that, distribute 20-25 kg of NPK fertilizer per hectare and then add urea at 100 kg per hectare, waiting seven days before harvest. Pull any strong striga plants from the field before they flower and destroy the striga plants. For variety advice see ICAT, and for a good-storage type such as Mucuna, choose it as a secondary crop.

history.content: fumier ou compost difference

draws.answer: The catalogue puts them in the same rotation as a trailer: manure is given as the first layer, then the slow rotting material of the compost, then a little wood ash on top of that. Compost is a slow rotting material, but the catalogue names the one made in a heap, plant residues trodden down, and the activators, topsoil, well rotted compost, Mycotri, as the activator, alongside wood ash, topsoil, and salt. So compost is a kind of manure made on a heap, and manure is a kind of compost made from animal droppings. They are not the same thing.

The catalogue gives both and the difference in its own definition: compost is the slow rotting of plant and animal debris, laid on the site of a former compost heap, and it names the methods for making it, in which the slow materials are chopped and stirred well. Fumigating is the other way of saying spraying, and it has the same answer: treatment with a pesticide is what it calls the application of chemicals for protection against pests, fungi and root problems, and it names three products: pharmaceuticals, fungicide and insecticide, and it asks that before any of it is applied that the roots be healthy and that the plant be vigorous. So the catalogue treats composting as making the materials last longer and as protecting them, and fumigating as using a product outside the heap.

history.content: I have a small lowland rice plot of half a hectare. After I put the seedlings in, how much fertilizer should I put and when?

draws.answer: You should apply NPK fertilizer at 150-200 kg per hectare, which is the same as 75-100 kg for your half-hectare. First raise the seedling's nitrogen demand by placing a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Then bring organic matter back with manure, compost or bury residues instead of burning them, since mineral fertilizer alone does not work on run-down soil. Weed the field at 15-25 days after planting and do the first weeding as soon as possible. For a proper soil analysis and the correct dose for your field, visit ICAT.

per_item.reference: Because enough is not something you can check at a glance, and water is the input where failure is fastest. The rule is that water is freely available at all times, the drinkers never empty, clean, served in the shade and renewed at least twice a day, and a count is what lets you know before you run out rather than after. The figures are per hundred: two siphon drinkers of 3.5 litres from 1 to 30 days, three of 3.5 litres from 30 to 45 days, three of 10 litres for the chickens, four of 10 litres for the adult layers. history.content: Why does the reference count drinkers per hundred birds instead of just saying enough water? Justify.

draws.answer: Because water is most often the thing that runs out first in a flock. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference states the rule of four drinkers of 10 litres per hundred birds, three of them for adults and three of them for chicks, and it puts the frequency in the same breath as feeding: clean water is among the four things to do every day, alongside feed, droppings and the site. It also says to watch the drinkers: a bird should be changing water at all times otherwise it dies.

Because water is where most birds die in a flock, and a good drinker is part of the rule. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference specifies 5 drinkers of 10 litres per hundred birds, three times a day, in adults and chicks, and that is not a quantity you can guess from a word. It also specifies the drinkers themselves, clean, served in the shade, renewed at least twice a day, and washed every day. Water becomes a problem when it is not present, when it is not clean, and when it is not washed, because that is what leads to disease spread. A drinker that is empty or dirty will see birds die before you even know it.

per_item.reference: You are dealing with tomato late blight. First, cut off any leaves or whole plants that show dark, water-soaked lesions and destroy them right away. Then widen the spacing between your tomato rows and add stakes so air can move through the canopy. After that, stop watering the tops of the tomato plants late in the day to keep the foliage dry. Plant a resistant tomato variety for the next season and, if the disease comes back, treat with an approved fungicide at the label rate. For the correct fungicide and dosage, go to ICAT.

history.content: My tomatoes have leaves that look soaked and turn black, and the fruit is rotting. What is happening?

draws.answer: You are dealing with tomato late blight. First, remove any infected plants or leaves and destroy them right away to stop the spread. Then space the remaining tomato plants further apart and stake them so air can move through the canopy, and stop watering from overhead late in the day. Plant a tomato variety that is resistant to late blight for the next cycle. If the disease continues, apply an approved fungicide at the label-recommended rate. For the correct fungicide and dosage, visit ICAT.

The problem is late blight on tomato plants. Remove and destroy any leaves or plants that are showing dark, water-soaked lesions and release them. Then space and stake the remaining plants to improve airflow. Avoid watering overhead late in the day so water does not touch the foliage. Plant a resistant tomato variety if you can. If the disease continues, use an approved fungicide at the labelled rate. You can obtain the fungicide and its rate from ICAT.

history.content: I sell birds all the time but at the end of the year I have nothing left.

draws.answer: You are selling too much and not enough at the same time, and the study has that as its own problem. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference sells the first harvest at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 30 bags, then buys back grain at 16,000 FCFA a bag for 20,000, then sells again at 20,000 for 25,000, then buys more grain at 17,000. So you are following the cycle twice. Look at your buyers before you set a date: the study's own second year projection sells 1,422 birds at 2,250 FCFA and 2,376 eggs at 100 FCFA, so keep the list of buyers before you set one. And hold your grain well, because the study counts 30 days of storage before sale at six months without losing its value.

Then look at how you end up with the birds first. The 2020 ICAT and PASA reference counts birds of sale among the products, alongside eggs and droppings, and it gives no number of birds sold, no profit per head and no cost per bird. So the question is whether you are selling every bird rather than the ones that are ill or weak, and that is a question for record keeping rather than for a thought on your table. What the reference does not say is what the birds represent: neither does the reference say how much feed a unit needs or what a bird is worth on the market, and either is a guess. If the birds are the whole, the answer is to plan before you buy: record every expense, work out the cost of production per head, decide the profit you want per head and compare that with the market price, and then readjust if the price moves. Look to ICAT for help building your own figures.

history.content: My tomato garden has a lot of weeds and the leaves look a bit sick, how can I find out if whiteflies or aphids are the cause?

draws.answer: First, shake a few tomato plants and examine the leaf undersides to see which insect is present. Then turn the leaves over and count the insects on several plants. If whiteflies dominate, set up yellow sticky traps to catch the adults; if aphids dominate, spray a strong jet of water on the plants and encourage ladybirds and lacewings. Remove the most infested leaves and destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. For a heavy attack, ask ICAT for the approved product and its rate.

Shake a plant and watch; if a cloud of tiny white insects flies up and then falls back down, whiteflies are likely causing damage. Turn the leaves over and count the insects on a few plants to be sure. Pick off the most infested leaves, destroy them, and keep the plot edges free of weeds that host the pests. Use yellow sticky traps for whiteflies, and a strong jet of water plus natural enemies like ladybirds or lacewings for aphids. For the approved spray and its rate, see ICAT.

per_item.reference: False, and this one is worth getting right because it changes everything you do. The catalogue says the reverse: replanting the trees is the first aim in time, and the crops are practised secondarily, for a limited period of two to three years, so as to let the trees grow well. It is a technique for places where land pressure is strong. That is why the crop sequence is fixed and short: cowpea, groundnut or pea the first year, then sorghum, millet or maize the two following years. After those two or three years the cropping stops. The trees used are teak, gmelina, which is called Indian teak, cashew, leucaena, acacia, senna and neem.

history.content: True or false: in the Taungya method the crop is the main aim and the trees are just there to help it.

draws.answer: False. The catalogue states the opposite: in Taungya the goal is to put a tree or a shade-loving plant in with the crops so that in a short time the cropping gives a first harvest and the trees grow well. The cropping is usually short-cycle varieties, 75 to 85 days, and is done under the shade of a powerful tree, which is the rule rather than an option.

False. The crops are only the first year aim, and the trees are the long-term goal. The catalogue says the crop cultivation runs parallel to the tree planting over a limited period of two to three years, so the trees are intended to shade and protect the crop for that time. It also gives the method's conditions: the land is usually semi-damp, poor rich, shallow, disturbed, with only 10 to 20 m of soil above, and it is carried out on a small area.

Keep the second weeding and earthing-up on schedule. If you see any streaks or dead-hearts, go to ICAT.

history.content: The lower leaves of my maize tunred yellow after the rain, but there are no streaks. What should I do?

draws.answer: Those streaks indicate nitrogen loss, so do not buy a broad-spectrum NPK compound or a systemic fungicide. First bring back organic matter by applying manure, compost, or leaving residues in the field rather than burning them. Then include a legume such as cowpea, groundnut or soybean in the rotation and cut the stems at ground level so the nitrogen-fixing nodules stay in the soil. Finally, ask ICAT for a soil analysis and the correct fertilizer dose for your plot. ICAT is the service to see.

history.content: I found many ticks on my cattle and some are dull and lagging. How should I act?

draws.answer: You should hand-pick every tick you see on all of your cattle, not just the dull, lagging ones. As you move through the herd, pull ticks from the ears, the tail and any animals with thinness. This is because the ticks left on the others will pass the parasite to them next. After you have removed the ticks, call the veterinary service the same day so they can tell you which disease you have and give the correct drug and dose. When you speak with the vet, describe the colour of the urine to help identify redwater or gall sickness. Keep any sick animal in the shade with clean water and do not make it walk. Do not use the same needle on two animals. The veterinary service is the only one you need to see for diagnosis and medication.

per_item.reference: Togo's five regions determine the pattern: Kara and Savanes in the north have one season, Maritime and Plateaux in the south have two seasons, and Centrale shows a blend. First, tell me which of the five regions your village belongs to. Then, if it is Kara or Savanes, use the single-season plan; if Maritime or Plateaux, use the double-season plan; if Centrale, expect a mixed pattern. After you state the region, contact ICAT for the prefecture-level calendar that gives the exact planting dates.

history.content: I'm unsure if my village follows the north or south planting pattern. How can I find out?

draws.answer: The north planting pattern follows a single rainy season from May through September. First, identify whether your village lies in Kara or Savanes, which has a single rainy season. If it does, plant at the start of the reliable rain period. If it does not, you are in the southern region, Maritime or Plateaux, where two rainy seasons apply. For detailed prefecture-level calendars, contact ICAT.

The north of Togo is Kara and Savanes, which follows a single-season planting pattern with one season. The south is Maritime and Plateaux, which follows a two-season pattern with two seasons. Centrale lies in the transition zone and can behave either way. For exact prefecture-level calendars, you should consult ICAT.

per_item.reference: A live hedge is what the catalogue offers for that: it is planted to keep animals, wind or light out. Dig a continuous trench along the line, 50 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a single line, or 60 cm wide and 60 cm deep for a double staggered line, which is the stronger of the two against animals. Plant by direct sowing, by cutting or from potted plants, with jatropha and thevetia often used between the trees. Then weed it and replace the plants that died for the two following seasons, because a hedge with gaps in it is a gap. Ask ICAT what is available as plants near you.

history.content: My plot backs onto the grazing land and the cattle come through the gap every dry season.

draws.answer: Two things to fix. First, the gap is what you are stopping, so go to ICAT and ask where this is a weakness in your layout rather than a lack of animals: the catalogue advises looking at the layout on a small area first and not filling in the whole plan before you look at the ground. Second, keep the crop in mind, because a windbreak planted against the dominant wind is a curtain of trees planted in lines, and that is the end of the catalogue's catalogue of what it offers. A line of trees planted in lines is also what the windbreak is meant to do, and it is a curtain of trees that stops the wind in one direction, not a barrier you step over.

That is the kind of problem the fenced run is meant to fix. The rule is one direction, and the run is the one way the animals should come: the 2020 ICAT and PASA reference says a fenced run for breeding, with the henhouse open on the worst of days, and it names the gaps as the ones to close, at eight to ten birds per square metre, one for about ten birds. What you have is a gap where they are not. Set a fenced run rather than a gap, and make it well followed, because that is what the run is for. Open a fenced run to the animals rather than letting them in at will.
